newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB chief economist sees no Swiss deflation danger.
newsitem.headline: SNB chief economist sees no Swiss deflation danger.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank's chief economist said he no longer saw a danger of Switzerland's static economy falling into deflation.
George Rich told a Swiss newspaper the prospect of a destructive downward spiral in prices had been banished by a more liberal monetary policy the SNB adopted in 1995.
"At that time (summer 1995) we saw the possibility of deflation. This danger was banished with a more liberal monetary policy," Rich told the weekly business paper HandelsZeitung.
The SNB cut its discount rate in four steps last year and again on September 26 in an effort to revive economic growth.
The discount rate fell from 3.5 percent at the start of 1995 to 1.5 percent by year's end and was slashed last month to a 20-year low of 1.0 percent.
But the Swiss economy is still struggling under a strong Swiss franc, weak European export markets and structural woes.
"The situation at the moment is gloomy. But I would not talk about deflation," Rich said.
SNB chairman Hans Meyer on October 18 forecast a decline of O.5 percent in Swiss gross domestic product (GDP) this year before a pick-up of between 1.0 and 1.5 percent next year.
Rich said he ruled out a deflationary danger because price declines were limited to some sectors rather than being generalised and continued over a longer period of time.
"This (falling prices) may be true in some cases, but overall neither prices nor wages are declining," he said.
Rich said his reference point for price developments was the Swiss consumer price index, which rose 0.2 percent from September to total 0.8 percent year-on-year in October.
Swiss average annual inflation should rise modestly to about 1.0 percent in 1997, the Federal Statistics Office forecast this week.
Rich repeated the SNB was not willing to risk long-term inflation by trying to weaken the high Swiss franc exchange rate with a massive boost in money supply.
"In the current constellation of exchange rates, this (lowering the Swiss franc) would mean significantly stronger growth in money supply," he said.
"We are not willing to accept this risk because we are duty-bound to consider the long-term effects of our policy," he added.
